Preamble

This subverse isn't about finding a Venge for $100, or about finding that set of SRAM Red for cheap, either. Just... no.

Generally, there's a limit to what you can find- e.g., go for really common stuff, and don't look for 'brand name.' If it's from China, it's best to assume it's a knockoff product and they've already let quality slip well below where it should be, below the quality of something that should be riddenon, especially for the sake of saving just a few bucks. What it is about, though is replacing your handlebar tape for under $3. Getting a set of cheap and functional lights. You might be a penny pincher, someone who likes getting a good deal on stuff that gets the job done for cheap, or maybe you're buying something for a neighbor, friend, or family member who picked up an old bike off a yard sale and it needs a part for cheap. Maybe you're a student, maybe you're just flat broke. Maybe you're a little concerned about them and know they're a bit careless about locking their bike and so you want a cheap but functional light so it won't be missed as badly when that 1cm cable lock gets snipped while they're inside or some such. Point is, that's what this sub's for and what this guide's for, and pointing out what designs work for you versus what ones are total flops.

Why eBay?

eBay has been pretty consistently good for me insofar as finding what I want for far cheaper than even my wholesaler can supply. The very same lights from the same factory with the exact same design and build quality with a difference of $2-$3 per light is considerable when you're running a business or a give-away in terms of the amount of good you can do for your target audience. Biking should be cheap and available to the masses. It's you, your bike, and whatever you ate for breakfast as your fuel.

Search Terms

"Bicycle" generally returns a lot of bicycle (The card company) knockoff products. "Bike" works pretty well, though, I do turn up some neat bicycle-themed jewelry and accoutrements that I've ordered for my roommate and I, she rocks it better though. I think the coolest I found was a welded bicycle-chain with a welded tab on it as a bottle opener for a couple bucks. Pretty neat. So sometimes you find random neat stuff this way anyways even if it's not strictly what you're looking for.

You can enter a "-" before a word you want to exclude. E.g., "Bicycle Light -Card" means that anything with the search term "card" might get excluded. However, eBay seems to allow a ridiculous number of tags on products on the off chance it's something vague or hard to describe. So excluding "card", (weirdly), has really messed with my search results for legit bike products.

Setup

So, you've entered your terms. Congrats- whether you're looking for a bike light, stickers, shifter cable, or whatever else, you've got vaguely in-mind what you're looking for. Check that the search return results are vaguely what you want- but don't click anything yet, we'll get there. If it's good, then let's proceed.

While auctions are certainly more fun and can certainly be worth it, we're haggling over a few cents here, oftentimes for a single item, and it takes literally more time than it's worth in terms of savings. If your item's worth $0.69 cents, then by haggling and getting it for $0.25 or even $0.01 has saved you less than the price of a bouncy ball at one of those coin vending machines. You literally make 8 of the difference, per hour, if you work minimum wage. If you make more, then it's an even bigger 'waste of time.' Though I'm not here to discourage you per se, I've never managed to snag an item off auction at closing for less than the 'buy it now' value.

So, let's switch to 'buy it now,' for the purposes of organization. Then let's select "price, lowest first." You may recognize that designs repeat themselves, over and over. Even the marketing photos are exactly the same. I think it's the same manufacturer, but different sellers clamoring for the same product from the factory's floor who are working a third shift and don't want it traced back to them directly. (China does that a lot, apparently. They'll put out extra product using their own materials, or somesuch, and then sell it locally, which I suppose in turn is selling it on eBay.)

I'm supposing that the fewer middlemen, the lower the price is.

Checkout

Anyways, also make certain that you've ticked the 'free shipping' tick mark and you're logged in. The "C" is a weird pseudo-currency that eBay seems to use- if anyone can clarify its purpose for me, feel free to do so. The US Dollar breaks out to be worth more per dollar, so if something is, say, C0.99, then it breaks out to be USD $0.69., it often provides a translation to the US Dollar that you'll be charged for the product. It does it above-board through paypal, which I've always found pretty comforting to know how much I'll be charged and that that's the agreed to amount. I've made the mistake of occasionally forgetting to check the 'free shipping' box and getting nailed with $7 shipping on a $1 piece of equipment.

Reminder

I would urge caution when ordering anything critical, such as a brake cable, handlebars, spoke, ball bearings, or so on and so forth. There is NO Quality Control beyond us on this, and those sorts of things failing on you can be catastrophic. Moreover, again, I'll repeat: while I know a lot of people tend to try and find a "deal" for their race bike, this isn't how you go about doing it. It works for me commuting with things like grips, but I wouldn't trust it for cables or anything 'brand name' unless you want a cheap knock-off that isn't half as good as what you're replacing.
